CASSINI-X — Beyond the Boundaries

We aim to explore Earth's environments and identify locations that resemble potential permanent settlement sites on the Moon and Mars. By combining scientific research, technology, creativity, and collaborative problem-solving, we seek to develop meaningful insights that support future space exploration.

Our Vision: To turn scientific curiosity into innovative solutions and help shape humanity's future beyond Earth.

Our Motto: Explore. Analyze. Innovate.
summary:
ASTRA-X, developed by team CASSINI-X, is an explainable, data-driven intelligence platform that solves a foundational challenge in space exploration: "Given a region of interest on Mars or the Moon, which locations on Earth possess comparable terrain characteristics?"

Historically, terrestrial analog sites for robotics testing and astronaut training were chosen ad hoc. ASTRA-X replaces subjective guesswork with rigorous quantitative science. Ingesting open orbital elevation rasters (NASA/USGS MOLA, LOLA, and SRTM), the platform standardizes spatial scale and extracts measurable morphometric features—including relative relief, slope gradients, and surface roughness. Candidates are ranked using a transparent weighted Euclidean similarity model alongside independent data-confidence scoring and traverse pathfinding.

ASTRA-X transforms planetary mission planning by providing verifiable, reproducible decision support, accelerating exploration readiness and operational rover qualification before hardware ever leaves Earth.

ASTRA-X — Complete Project Dossier

Platform: ASTRA-X — Planetary Terrestrial Analog Discovery Platform
Team: CASSINI-X
Tagline: "Discover Earth. Understand Other Worlds. Prepare for Exploration."

Project Summary

ASTRA-X, developed by team CASSINI-X, is a data-driven web application that answers a crucial question in space exploration: "Given a selected region on Mars or the Moon, which locations on Earth have comparable terrain characteristics?" Historically, terrestrial analog sites for rover testing and astronaut training were chosen ad hoc. ASTRA-X replaces subjective guesswork with a quantitative, repeatable standard. It ingests open orbital elevation datasets from NASA and USGS, standardizes them onto a unified spatial grid, extracts measurable physical terrain features, and ranks Earth candidate locations using a transparent weighted-distance model with independent confidence scoring. Every match comes with a clear, feature-by-feature explanation so mission planners can inspect and verify why a site was selected.

How It Works

ASTRA-X operates through a transparent five-stage pipeline:

Stage 1 — Planetary Data Ingestion: The system ingests authentic open planetary elevation rasters — NASA/USGS MOLA for Mars (128 px/deg), LOLA for the Moon (118 m/px), and SRTM for Earth (30 m / 1 arc-sec). These are real satellite-derived digital elevation models, not simulated data.

Stage 2 — Spatial Standardization & Feature Extraction: Raw altimetry is resampled onto a uniform 500-meter grid to resolve planetary datum differences. Three physically grounded morphometric features are computed: (1) Relative Elevation — detrended residual relief removing planetary sea-level bias, (2) Horn Slope — two-dimensional finite-difference surface gradient in degrees, and (3) Surface Roughness — local standard deviation of elevation across a 5×5 kernel window.

Stage 3 — Similarity Engine & Spatial ML: Candidate Earth regions are evaluated using an inverted normalized weighted Euclidean distance in standardized feature space. Unsupervised machine learning provides additional insight through Silhouette-optimized K-Means clustering, DBSCAN spatial density grouping, and Isolation Forest anomaly detection to surface morphologically unique terrain.

Stage 4 — Tripartite Scoring: Three independent metrics are strictly separated across the entire system — Similarity Score (physical terrain match percentage), Confidence Score (data coverage fraction and resolution ratio), and Mission Suitability Score (preliminary landing slope hazard screening). These are never merged, ensuring data gaps cannot be confused with terrain safety.

Stage 5 — Decision Support & Reporting: The platform provides 8-connected A* rover pathfinding with slope hazard avoidance and elevation profile charts, plus automated publication-ready PDF scientific dossiers with full data provenance tables.

Project Highlights

Key Statistics (Real, Verified Numbers)

  • 11 pages across the full-stack application
  • 61 frontend React components across 10,858 lines of TypeScript
  • 35 backend Python modules across 4,839 lines of code
  • 11 scientific analysis modules (features, similarity, clustering, anomaly, pathfinding, confidence, validation, normalization, search, visualization, engine)
  • 7 REST API router groups (system, regions, analysis, mission, reports, assistant, gazetteer)
  • 49 automated backend tests (all passing)
  • 7 processed planetary elevation tiles (Mars Jezero, Mars Olympus, Moon Tranquillitatis, Moon Shackleton, Earth Atacama, Earth Haughton, Earth Lanzarote)
  • 4,147 terrestrial candidate cells evaluated per analysis run
  • 50+ scientific PDF reports generated and archived
  • 3 benchmark validation pairs calibrated against peer-reviewed analog literature

Important Notes & Scientific Integrity

Scientific Honesty Protocol (Strictly Enforced)

  1. Zero Data Fabrication — Every number shown is computed from real open planetary datasets or clearly labeled as DEMO DATA in demo mode.
  2. Metric Separation — Similarity, Confidence, and Mission Suitability are three independent fields everywhere (database, API, UI, reports). They are never merged.
  3. No Safety Claims — The platform never states that a site is "safe for landing." Suitability output is labeled "preliminary screening for decision support only."
  4. No Identity Claims — Results say "comparable on the selected features," never "identical to Mars."
  5. Explicit Data Gaps — Missing raster cells are masked, not filled. Coverage fraction is displayed as a data quality indicator.

Open Data Sources & Attribution

  • Mars Elevation: NASA/USGS Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) — Mars Global Surveyor
  • Moon Elevation: NASA/USGS Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
  • Earth Elevation: NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) GL1 — 30m resolution
  • Earth Visualization: NASA Visible Earth Blue Marble — cloud-free satellite composite
  • Moon Visualization: LRO WAC Mosaic — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera
  • All datasets are publicly available through NASA PDS, USGS Astrogeology, and AWS Open Data Registry.

Benchmark Validation Results

The similarity model was validated against 3 established planetary analog benchmark pairs from peer-reviewed literature:

  • Devon Island (Haughton Crater) ↔ Jezero Crater Floor: Ranked #2 out of 4,147 candidates (95.68% similarity)
  • Lanzarote Volcanic Field ↔ Mare Tranquillitatis: Ranked #16 out of 4,147 candidates (93.49% similarity)
  • Mauna Kea & Kilauea ↔ Mare Tranquillitatis: Expected negative control, ranked #3,787 (10.56% similarity — correctly identified as non-analog)

Creativity & Innovation

  1. Cross-Planetary Altimetric Normalization — Solves the multi-body datum problem by comparing detrended local relief rather than absolute altitude, which would fail across planets with different radiuses and no shared sea level.
  2. Aerospace-Grade Interactive UX — Features a cinematic Three.js 3D scene with a photorealistic rotating Earth, orbiting Moon, multi-colored twinkling starfield, and SpaceX-inspired bold typography — all rendered in real-time WebGL.
  3. Explainability-First AI — Instead of opaque deep learning that cannot explain its predictions, every similarity score provides an exact mathematical decomposition showing which terrain feature contributed to the match and by how much.
  4. Integrated Mission Planning — Goes beyond mere similarity discovery to provide operational rover traverse optimization using A* pathfinding with slope gradient constraints, directly supporting real mission hardware qualification.

Intended Impact

  • De-risks Planetary Hardware: Enables roboticists to test rovers and instruments on Earth terrains that mathematically mirror Martian and lunar environments.
  • Optimizes Mission Budgets: Eliminates wasteful ad-hoc field site scouting, saving aerospace programs significant logistical costs.
  • Accelerates Astronaut Training: Identifies accessible, geologically relevant training grounds for Artemis lunar surface crews.
  • Democratizes Planetary Science: Bridges open NASA/USGS data archives into an accessible, explainable tool for students, researchers, and space agencies worldwide.

Live Deployment

  • Frontend (Vercel): Globally distributed via Edge CDN with automatic HTTPS
  • Backend API (Render): Python FastAPI service with continuous deployment from GitHub
  • Source Code (GitHub): github.com/Karthick-2307/CASSINI-X

Developed by Team CASSINI-X | All planetary datasets courtesy of NASA, USGS Astrogeology Science Center, and AWS Open Data Registry.
